column4: The section names the Zaqqūm tree as the source of the condemned meal; this verse frames that tree as the alternative to a better reception, making the meal itself a reversal of welcome.
The section identifies Zaqqūm as the food of the scene; this verse says the tree was made a trial for wrongdoers, explaining its role as an ordeal rather than nourishment.
This neighbor locates the same Zaqqūm tree in the depths of Hell, adding the source's setting to the section's cited eating scene.
This neighbor describes the Zaqqūm tree's emerging fruit as like devils' heads, supplying a concrete detail of the plant named in the section.
After the section's cited Zaqqūm meal and drink, this verse calls the sequence the sinners' reception on Judgment Day, identifying the meal as their allotted provision.
The section cites 77:31's shade that cannot protect; this preceding verse directs the deniers toward that apparent shade, setting up the failed refuge.
The section cites the deniers' ineffective shade in 77:31; this verse gives the God-fearing shade and springs, a specific effective counterpart.
The section's food leaves hunger unmet; this continuation gives the God-fearing fruit they desire, the nourishing counterpart in the same surah's afterlife scene.
The section cites food that does not satisfy; this verse tells the God-fearing to eat and drink pleasantly, a direct reversal of the failed meal.

The section's secondary dictionary sense of ضريع includes a sheep with a large udder and a thin drink; this verse describes pure, palatable milk from livestock, a specific counterimage of drink and nourishment.

The section's dictionary sense of ضريع includes a large-udder sheep; this verse names cattle as drink, food, and many benefits, contrasting usable provision with the dry plant that does neither bodily job.

The section's named root جوع describes hunger left unresolved; this verse permits otherwise forbidden food for someone in severe hunger, showing food preserving life where the section's sole food cannot.

The section names root غ ن ي and its sense of sufficiency; this verse portrays one who withholds and considers himself free of need, a false sufficiency set against the image's real, unrelieved hunger.

The section's dictionary phrase طاعم حسن الحال links eating with bodily well-being; this verse says messengers were bodies that ate, marking ordinary food as part of embodied life and the condemned meal as a reversal.

The section's dictionary phrase طاعم حسن الحال connects eating with good condition; this verse repeats the human-messenger image of eating food and walking markets, making the section's failed nourishment a counterfeit of ordinary life.
The section gives ضريع the secondary dictionary sense of a thin drink; this verse explicitly turns attention to the water people drink, connecting that branch to bodily need.
This continuation asks who sent down the water named in 56:68, adding the source of drink to the section's secondary dictionary sense of ضريع as a beverage.
This continuation says the drinking water could have been made bitter; it marks the boundary between drink that can relieve need and the section's intake that cannot.
